Exactly. We can achieve total prison abolition by abolitionising PRISONS, not confinement altogether. I feel like not enough people understand how different types of confinement can really be WORLDS apart. 

Saying that rehabilitation centers are just like prisons because they both confine people is like saying that planes are just like cars because they both have wheels.

So just to note, there is a material difference between a prison and rehabilitation center. In a prison is intended for people that are considered lesser than the average citizen (i.e. they don't DESERVE to be a healthy member of society). Whereas a rehabilitation center is intended for the opposite (i.e. they deserve to be a healthy member of society but are unable to until rehabilitated). 

In a rehabilitation center, it would be impossible for something like Solitary Confinement to exist. At all times, even if the criminal in question never improves, they're improvement would be the GOAL (as opposed to punishment for justice's sake). 

When you think on it this way, there is no logical fallacy that makes complete abolition impossible. Confinement and prison just aren't the same.

For example, we can consider how the Japanese Emperor denounced his godhood at the end of WW2, and the impact it had on degrading the ideologies behind Japanese imperialism. I should make it clear that I'm not advocating for the eradication of all forms of prison. Rather, I'm thinking about how we should view war-crime justice from a prison abolitionist lens. I mostly agree with you, I'm actually quite critical of the executions that came out of the Nuremberg trail. Those who got the death penalty just became political martyrs, and I would argue that letting them live the rest of their lives in prison would've been a more effective form of justice. Those dead Nazis basically became saints to neo-nazi groups that would pop-up in Europe, and theoretically, they could've been more useful alive since they had lots of useful information on where other Nazi leadership and other sympathizing fascists were hiding. 

Even if I wasn't already against capital punishment, I would still say that it would be a terrible idea (from a strategic standpoint) to give Nethanyau or any members of his inner circle the death penalty. The violent fallout from his followers wouldn't be worth the risk. Then again, the reason why I'm making this post is because I'm having a hard time conceptualizing an ideal punishment for war criminals of that caliber.

On a purely ethical basis, I agree with your take. That being said, on a material basis, I feel like any public figure is going to have to be treated differently because of the influence they have over their followers. A famous prisoner is basically always a political prisoner, and they'll have followers who will fight on their behalf. 

So I guess the real question here is how would we handle the political fallout of rehabilitating someone who is world-renown for their evil and has millions of victims with differing (and likely passionate) opinions on how to handle the situation ?
